'''''Rosa canina''''', the '''dog rose''',<ref name=RHS>{{cite web |title=Rosa canina (S) dog rose |publisher=Royal Horticultural Society |url=https://www.rhs.org.uk/Plants/16017/i-Rosa-canina-i-(S)/Details|access-date=2017-04-04}}</ref> is a variable climbing, wild [[rose]] species native to Europe, northwest Africa, and western Asia.

==Description==
The dog rose is a [[deciduous]] shrub normally ranging in height from {{convert|1–5|m|ft|frac=2}}, though it can scramble higher into the crowns of taller trees. Its multiple arching stems<ref name="USDA"/> are covered with small, sharp, hooked [[thorns, spines, and prickles|prickles]], which aid it in climbing. The leaves are [[pinnate]], with 5–7 leaflets,<ref>{{Cite web|title=Burke Herbarium Image Collection|url=http://biology.burke.washington.edu/herbarium/imagecollection/taxon.php?Taxon=Rosa%20canina|access-date=2021-11-26|website=biology.burke.washington.edu}}</ref> and have a delicious fragrance when bruised.<ref>{{Cite book |last=Genders |first=Roy |title=Scented flora of the world |date=1994 |publisher=Hale |isbn=0-7090-5440-8 |edition=1st paperback|location=London |oclc=33964778}}</ref>

[[Image:Aestivation.png|thumb|upright|left|Quincuncial [[aestivation (botany)|aestivation]] (A)]]
[[File:Rosa canina 244689792.jpg|thumb|Close-up of [[rose hip]]s]]

The dog rose blooms from June to July, with sweet-scented flowers that are usually pale pink, but can vary between a deep pink and white. They are {{convert|4|–|6|cm|frac=2}} in diameter with five petals. Like other roses it has a quincuncial [[aestivation (botany)|aestivation]]. Unusually though, of its five [[sepal]]s, when viewed from underneath, two are whiskered (or 'bearded') on both sides, two are quite smooth and one is whiskered on one side only.<ref name="stearn">{{Cite book |last=William T. Stearn |url=https://www.huntbotanical.org/admin/uploads/11hibd-huntia-2-pp180-184.pdf |title=The five bretheren of the rose: An old botanical riddle |publisher=Huntia Volume 2 |year=1965 |volume=2 |location=Pittsburgh |pages=180–184}}</ref>{{rp|182}} It has usually 10 or more [[pistil]]s, and multiple [[stamen]]s.<ref name="USDA"/>

Flowers mature in September to October,<ref name="USDA"/> into an oval, {{convert|1.5–2|cm|abbr=on|frac=4}}, red-orange [[rose hip|hips]].<ref name="Fujii2009">{{cite journal |last1=Fujii |first1=Takashi |last2=Saito |first2=Morio |title=Inhibitory effect of quercetin isolated from rose hip (''Rosa canina'' L.) against melanogenesis by mouse melanoma cells |journal=Biosci. Biotechnol. Biochem. |date=September 2009 |volume=73 |issue=9 |pages=1989–93 |doi=10.1271/bbb.90181 |pmid=19734679|doi-access=free }}</ref> The fruits can persist on the plant for several months (if not eaten by wildlife) and become black.<ref name="USDA"/><ref>{{cite book |last1=Young |first1=J.A. |last2=Young |first2=C.G. |title=Seeds of Woody Plants of North America. |date=1992 |publisher=Disocorides Press |location=Portland, OR.}}</ref>
[[File:Bloem van een Rosa canina 01-06-2026. (actm.).jpg |thumb|250px| inflorescence]]

Its fruit [[persistence (botany)|persists]] for an average of 64 days, and bears an average of 18.1 seeds per fruit. Fruits average 65.2% water (possibly the lowest water content among European fleshy fruits), and their [[dry matter|dry weight]] includes 17.3% [[carbohydrate]]s and 0.7% [[lipid]]s.{{sfn|Ehrlén|Eriksson|1991}}

Its form and flowers can be confused with fieldbriar ''[[Rosa agrestis]]'' and sweetbriar ''[[Rosa rubiginosa]]''.

===Genetics===
Dog roses have an unusual kind of [[meiosis]] which is sometimes called permanent odd [[polyploidy]], although it can also occur with even polyploidy (e.g. in tetraploids or hexaploids). Regardless of [[ploidy]] level, only seven [[bivalent (genetics)|bivalent]]s are formed leaving the other chromosomes as univalents. Univalents are included in [[egg cell]]s, but not in [[pollen]].<ref>{{cite journal | last1 = Täckholm | first1 = Gunnar | year = 1922 | title = Zytologische Studien über die Gattung ''Rosa'' | journal = Acta Horti Bergiani | volume = 7 | pages = 97–381 }}</ref><ref>{{cite journal |doi=10.1038/sj.hdy.6800648 |pmid=15770234 |title=Evolutionary implications of permanent odd polyploidy in the stable sexual, pentaploid of ''Rosa canina'' L |journal=Heredity |volume=94 |issue=5 |pages=501–506 |year=2005 |last1=Lim |first1=K Y |last2=Werlemark |first2=G |last3=Matyasek |first3=R |last4=Bringloe |first4=J B |last5=Sieber |first5=V |last6=El Mokadem |first6=H |last7=Meynet |first7=J |last8=Hemming |first8=J |last9=Leitch |first9=A R |last10=Roberts |first10=A V |bibcode=2005Hered..94..501L |doi-access=free }}</ref> Similar processes occur in some other organisms.<ref>{{cite journal |doi=10.1098/rspb.2011.1738 |title=Simultaneous Mendelian and clonal genome transmission in a sexually reproducing, all-triploid vertebrate |journal=Proceedings of the Royal Society B: Biological Sciences |volume=279 |issue=1732 |pages=1293–9 |year=2011 |last1=Stock |first1=M. |last2=Ustinova |first2=J. |last3=Betto-Colliard |first3=C. |last4=Schartl |first4=M. |last5=Moritz |first5=C. |last6=Perrin |first6=N. |pmid=21993502 |pmc=3282369}}</ref> Dog roses ([[Rosa sect. Caninae|''Rosa'' sect. ''Caninae'']]) are most commonly [[pentaploid]], i.e. with five times the base number of seven chromosomes for the genus ''[[rose|Rosa]]'', but may be [[diploid]], [[tetraploid]] or [[hexaploid]] as well.<ref>{{citation |title=Evolutionary implications of permanent odd polyploidy in the stable sexual, pentaploid of ''Rosa canina'' L. |author=K Y Lim, G Werlemark, R Matyasek, J B Bringloe, V Sieber, H El Mokadem, J Meynet, J Hemming, A R Leitch & A V Roberts |journal=Heredity |year=2005 |volume=94 |issue=5 |pages=501–506 |doi=10.1038/sj.hdy.6800648 |bibcode=2005Hered..94..501L }}</ref>

==Taxonomy==
[[Image:Illustration Rosa canina1.jpg|thumb|upright|Botanical illustration by [[Otto Wilhelm Thomé]]]]

Classical writers did not recognise ''Rosa canina'' as a rose, but called it ''Cynorrhodon'', from the Greek κυνόροδον. In 1538, Turner called it "Cynosbatos : wild hep or brere tree". Yet in 1551, [[Matthias de l'Obel]] classified it as a rose, under the name, "Canina Rosa odorata et silvestris", in his herbal "Rubus canis: Brere bush or hep tree" .<ref name="willmott">{{Cite book |last=Willmott, Ellen Ann, Parsons, Alfred |url=https://www.biodiversitylibrary.org/item/213425#page/212/mode/1up |title=The genus rosa |publisher=John Murray |year=1914 |volume=2 |location=London |pages=212 |doi=10.5962/bhl.title.106082}}</ref>

Based on a 2013 [[DNA]] analysis using [[amplified fragment length polymorphism]]s of wild-rose samples from a transect across Europe (900 samples from section ''[[Rosa sect. Caninae|Caninae]]'', and 200 from other sections), it has been suggested that the following named species are best considered as belonging to a single ''R. canina'' species complex:<ref>{{cite journal |doi=10.1016/j.ympev.2013.02.024 |pmid=23499615 |title=AFLP-based population structure analysis as a means to validate the complex taxonomy of dog roses (''Rosa'' section ''Caninae'') |journal=Molecular Phylogenetics and Evolution |volume=67 |issue=3 |pages=547–559 |year=2013 |last1=De Riek |first1=Jan |last2=De Cock |first2=Katrien |last3=Smulders |first3=Marinus J.M. |last4=Nybom |first4=Hilde |bibcode=2013MolPE..67..547D |url=https://library.wur.nl/WebQuery/wurpubs/437653 |url-access=subscription }}</ref>
* ''R. balsamica'' <small>Besser</small>
* ''R. caesia'' <small>Sm.</small>
* ''R. corymbifera'' <small>Borkh.</small>
* ''[[Rosa dumalis|R. dumalis]]'' <small>Bechst.</small>
* ''R. montana'' <small>Chaix</small>
* ''R. stylosa'' <small>Desv.</small>
* ''R. subcanina'' <small>(Christ) Vuk.</small>
* ''R. subcollina'' <small>(Christ) Vuk.</small>
* ''R.'' × ''irregularis'' <small>Déségl. & Guillon</small>

===Etymology===
The botanical name is derived from the common names 'dog rose' or similar in several European languages, including classical Latin and ancient (Hellenistic period) Greek.
The Roman naturalist [[Pliny the Elder|Pliny]] attributed the name dog rose to a belief that the plant's root could cure the bite of a mad dog. It is not clear if the dogs were [[rabies|rabid]].<ref>{{cite journal |last1=Haas |first1=L F |title=Rosa canina (dog rose). |journal=Journal of Neurology, Neurosurgery, and Psychiatry |volume=59 |issue=5 |pages=470 |date=November 1995|pmc=1073704 |pmid=8530926 |doi=10.1136/jnnp.59.5.470 }}</ref> According to ''The Oxford Dictionary of Phrase and Fable'',<ref>{{cite book |author=Elizabeth Knowles |title=The Oxford Dictionary of Phrase and Fable |chapter=Dog |edition=2nd |year=2005 |publisher=[[Oxford University Press]] |isbn=978-0-19-860981-0 |url-access=registration |url=http://www.oxfordreference.com/view/10.1093/acref/9780198609810.001.0001/acref-9780198609810-e-2185?rskey=tkVbzl&result=2}}</ref> the English name is a direct translation of the plant's name from classical Latin, ''rosa canina'', itself a translation of the Greek κυνόροδον ('kunórodon'); It is thought to have been used to treat the bite of rabid dogs in the 18th and 19th centuries.<ref>Howard, Michael. ''Traditional Folk Remedies'' (Century, 1987); p.133</ref> The origin of its name may be related to the hooked prickles on the plant that have resemblance to a dog's canines.<ref>{{cite web |title=Properties of dog rose |url=https://www.botanical-online.com/en/medicinal-plants/dog-rose-rosa-canina-properties |website=Botanical online |access-date=21 November 2019 |date=19 January 2019}}</ref> It is sometimes considered that the word 'dog' has a disparaging meaning in this context, indicating 'worthless' as compared with cultivated garden roses.<ref>{{Cite book|url=https://archive.org/details/treesbushesinwoo0000vede|title=Trees and bushes in wood and hedgerow|last=Vedel, Helge.|orig-date=1960|type= reprint |year=1962|publisher=Methuen|others=Lange, Johan.|isbn=0-416-61780-8|location=London|oclc=863361796|url-access=registration}}</ref>

==Ecology==
===Pests and diseases===
[[File:Robin's pincushion on dog rose - geograph.org.uk - 1012403.jpg|thumb|upright|[[Rose bedeguar gall]] on a dog rose]]

The dog rose can be attacked by aphids, [[leafhopper]]s, glasshouse [[red spider mite]], scale insects, caterpillars, rose leaf-rolling sawfly, and [[leaf-cutting bee]]s.<ref name="pfaf"/>

When a [[Diplolepis rosae|gall wasp]] lays eggs into a leaf axillary or terminal bud the plant develops a chemically induced distortion known as ''[[robin's pincushion]]''.<ref name="USDA"/>

Buds and leaves may be eaten by rabbits and deer, despite the thorns.<ref name="pfaf"/>

It may be affected by [[rose rust]] and [[powdery mildew]]s (''[[Podosphaera pannosa]]''),<ref name=RHS/> and downy mildew (''[[Peronospora sparsa]]'').<ref name="USDA"/>

It is notably susceptible to [[honey fungus]].<ref name="huxley">{{Cite book |last=Huxley |first=A |title=The New RHS Dictionary of Gardening. |publisher=Macmillan Press |year=1992 |isbn=0-333-47494-5 |location=London |oclc=25202760}}</ref>

===As an invasive species===
Dog rose is an [[invasive species]] in the [[High country (New Zealand)|high country]] of [[New Zealand]]. It was recognised as displacing native vegetation as early as 1895<ref>{{cite journal |last=Kirk |first=T |year=1895 |title=The Displacement of Species in New Zealand |journal=Transactions of the New Zealand Institute |publisher=Royal Society of New Zealand |location=Wellington |volume=28 |url=http://rsnz.natlib.govt.nz/volume/rsnz_28/rsnz_28_00_000440.html |access-date=2009-04-17}}</ref> although the [[Department of Conservation (New Zealand)|Department of Conservation]] does not consider it to be a conservation threat.<ref>{{cite book |last=Owen |first=S. J. |title=Ecological weeds on conservation land in New Zealand: a database |publisher=Department of Conservation |location=Wellington |year=1997}}</ref>

The dog rose is classified as a [[weed]] in Australia under the Natural Resources Management Act of 2004. It outcompetes native plants, offers shelter to pests like [[Feral foxes in Australia|foxes]] and [[Rabbits in Australia|rabbits]], is not eaten by livestock due to its unpalatable nature, and its large shrubs resist grazing by farm animals. The dog rose invades native [[bushland]] therefore reducing biodiversity and the presence of desirable pasture species.<ref>{{Cite web |last=Water (DEW) |first=Department for Environment and landscape |date=2019-01-29 |title=Who let the dog (rose) out? |url=https://www.landscape.sa.gov.au/lc/news/190121-dog_rose |access-date=2021-11-15 |website=www.landscape.sa.gov.au |language=en}}</ref> It is a biosecurity risk as it hosts fruit fly.<ref>{{Cite web |title=Wild rose |url=http://www.flora.sa.gov.au/cgi-bin/speciesfacts_display.cgi?genus=Rosa&species=canina |access-date=21 November 2019 |publisher=Government of South Australia}}</ref>
 
In the US, it is classified as a weed and invasive in some regions or habitats, where it may displace desirable vegetation due to its large size and
ability of regeneration from sprouts. It can also impede the movement of livestock, wildlife and vehicles.<ref name="USDA"/>

Birds and wild fruit eating animals are the main cause of seed dispersal. The plant seeds can also be carried in the hooves or fur of stock animals. They may also be carried by waterways.<ref>{{cite web |title=Pest plant - Dog rose and sweet briar rose - Department of Environment, Water and Natural Resources |url=https://www.naturalresources.sa.gov.au/samurraydarlingbasin/publications/pest-plant-dog-rose-and-sweet-briar-rose |website=www.naturalresources.sa.gov.au |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20190419205949/https://www.naturalresources.sa.gov.au/samurraydarlingbasin/publications/pest-plant-dog-rose-and-sweet-briar-rose |access-date=19 November 2019|archive-date=2019-04-19 }}</ref>

==Cultivation==
The dog rose is hardy to zone 3 in the UK ([[USDA hardiness zone]] 3–7), tolerates maritime exposure, grows well in a sunny position, and grows even in heavy clay soils, but like all roses dislikes water-logged soils or very dry sites. In deep shade, it usually fails to flower and fruit.<ref name="pfaf">{{Cite web |date=n.d. |title=''Rosa canina'' Dog Rose PFAF Plant Database |url=https://pfaf.org/user/plant.aspx?LatinName=Rosa+canina |access-date=2021-11-15 |website=pfaf.org}}</ref>

Numerous [[cultivar]]s have been named, though few are common in cultivation. The cultivar ''Rosa canina'' 'Assisiensis' is the only dog rose without thorns. Thought to be linked to [[Saint Francis of Assisi]], hence the name.<ref>{{cite web |title=A Rose Without Thorns in Assisi… |url=https://www.caftours.com/magazine/rose-thorns/index.html |website=CafTours Magazine |access-date=8 October 2023 |language=en-EN |date=27 May 2013}}</ref>

==Uses==
[[File:Ucierane_platki_rozy_z_Krasiczyna.jpg|thumb|upright|Crushing rose petals for jam]]

The fruits can be picked and eaten straight from the bush when ripe in autumn, if care is taken to avoid the hairs inside the fruit. They are also used to make syrup, tea, and preserves (jam and marmalade), and are used in the making of pies, stews, and wine. The flowers can be made into a syrup, eaten in salads, candied, or preserved in vinegar, honey or brandy.<ref>{{cite web |title=Rosehip - A Foraging Guide to Its Food and Medicine |url=https://www.eatweeds.co.uk/rosehip-rosa-canina |website=EATWEEDS |access-date=18 November 2019 |date=2 December 2018}}</ref> During [[World War II]] in the United States, ''Rosa canina'' was planted in [[victory garden]]s; it can still be found growing throughout that country, including on roadsides, in pastures and nature conservation areas.<ref name="USDA">{{cite web |last1=Pavek |first1=P.L.S. |title=DOG ROSE ''Rosa canina'' L. Plant Symbol = ROCA3 |url=https://plants.usda.gov/DocumentLibrary/plantguide/pdf/pg_roca3.pdf |website=plants.usda.gov |publisher=USDA-Natural Resources Conservation Service, Pullman, WA. |access-date=8 October 2023 |date=November 2012}}</ref>

In [[Poland]], the petals are used to make a jam that is particularly suitable for filling [[pączki]], a type of doughnut.<ref>{{cite web |title=Pączki Are the Stuffed Polish Doughnuts You Need to Know About |url=https://www.thekitchn.com/paczki-recipe-23123585|website=kitchn|access-date=14 November 2022 |date=16 January 2019}}</ref><ref>{{cite web |title=The Hirshon Polish Jelly Donuts for Fat Tuesday – Pączki |url=https://www.thefooddictator.com/the-hirshon-polish-jelly-donuts-for-fat-tuesday-paczki/|website=The Food Dictator|access-date=14 November 2022 |date=16 January 2019}}</ref>

Rose hip essential oil is composed mainly of alcohols, [[monoterpene]]s and [[sesquiterpene]]s.<ref>{{cite journal |last1=Ahmad |first1=Naveed |last2=Anwar |first2=Farooq |last3=Gilani |first3=Anwar-ul-Hassan |title=Chapter 76 - Rose Hip (Rosa canina L.) Oils |url=https://www.sciencedirect.com/science/article/pii/B9780124166417000766 |journal=Essential Oils in Food Preservation, Flavor and Safety |publisher=Academic Press |access-date=20 November 2019 |pages=667–675 |date=1 January 2016|doi=10.1016/B978-0-12-416641-7.00076-6 |isbn=9780124166417 |url-access=subscription }}</ref>

In [[Bulgaria]], where the dog rose grows in abundance, its hips are used to make sweet wine and tea.<ref>{{cite journal |last1=Rusanova |first1=M. |last2=Rusanov |first2=K. |last3=Stanev |first3=S. |last4=Kovacheva |first4=N. |last5=Atanassov |first5=I. |title=Total phenol content, antioxidant activity of hip extracts and genetic diversity in a small population of ''R. canina'' L. cv. Plovdiv 1 obtained by seed propagation. |journal=Agricultural Science and Technology. |date=2015 |volume=7 |issue=2 |pages=162–166}}</ref>

In [[Slovenia]], its hips are made into a popular drink named [[Cockta]].

===Nutritional value===
Rose hips (the pseudo-fruits of Rosa canina) are rich sources of vitamin C, which can vary widely depending on species, ripeness, and post-harvest handling.<ref>{{cite journal |last=Patel |first=Seema |title=Rose hip as an underutilized functional food: Evidence-based review |journal=Trends in Food Science & Technology |volume=63 |pages=29–38 |year=2017 |doi=10.1016/j.tifs.2017.03.001 |url=https://doi.org/10.1016/j.tifs.2017.03.001 |access-date=2025-10-06|url-access=subscription }}</ref> They also contain provitamin-A carotenoids, such as β-carotene and lutein, which contribute to antioxidant activity.<ref>{{cite journal |last1=Winther |first1=K |last2=Vinther Hansen |first2=AS |last3=Campbell-Tofte |first3=J |title=Bioactive ingredients of rose hips (Rosa canina L.) with special reference to antioxidative and anti-inflammatory properties: in vitro studies |journal=Botanics: Targets and Therapy |volume=2016 |pages=11–23 |year=2016 |doi=10.2147/BTAT.S91385 |doi-access=free |url=https://www.dovepress.com/bioactive-ingredients-of-rose-hips-rosa-canina-l-with-special-referenc-peer-reviewed-fulltext-article-BTAT |access-date=2025-10-06}}</ref> Tocopherols (vitamin E) are also present and contribute to the fruit’s antioxidant capacity.<ref>{{cite journal |last1=Mármol |first1=Inés |last2=Sánchez-de-Diego |first2=Cristina |last3=Jiménez-Moreno |first3=Nerea |last4=Ancín-Azpilicueta |first4=Carmen |last5=Rodríguez-Yoldi |first5=María Jesús |title=Therapeutic applications of rose hips from different Rosa species |journal=International Journal of Molecular Sciences |volume=18 |issue=6 |year=2017 |page=1137 |doi=10.3390/ijms18061137 |doi-access=free |pmid=28587101 |pmc=5485961 }}</ref> Phenolic compounds, including flavonoids and phenolic acids, provide additional antioxidant and anti-inflammatory properties.<ref>{{cite journal |last=Patel |first=Seema |title=Rose hip as an underutilized functional food: Evidence-based review |journal=Trends in Food Science & Technology |volume=63 |pages=29–38 |year=2017 |doi=10.1016/j.tifs.2017.03.001 |url=https://doi.org/10.1016/j.tifs.2017.03.001 |access-date=2025-10-06|url-access=subscription }}</ref> Essential minerals are also found in both the hypanthium and the seeds.<ref>{{cite journal |last1=Winther |first1=K |last2=Vinther Hansen |first2=AS |last3=Campbell-Tofte |first3=J |title=Bioactive ingredients of rose hips (Rosa canina L.) with special reference to antioxidative and anti-inflammatory properties: in vitro studies |journal=Botanics: Targets and Therapy |volume=2016 |pages=11–23 |year=2016 |doi=10.2147/BTAT.S91385 |doi-access=free |url=https://www.dovepress.com/bioactive-ingredients-of-rose-hips-rosa-canina-l-with-special-referenc-peer-reviewed-fulltext-article-BTAT |access-date=2025-10-06}}</ref>

The seeds contain an oil rich in polyunsaturated fatty acids, especially linoleic acid (35–56% of total fatty acids) and α-linolenic acid (20–30%).<ref>{{cite journal |last1=Winther |first1=K |last2=Vinther Hansen |first2=AS |last3=Campbell-Tofte |first3=J |title=Bioactive ingredients of rose hips (Rosa canina L.) with special reference to antioxidative and anti-inflammatory properties: in vitro studies |journal=Botanics: Targets and Therapy |volume=2016 |pages=11–23 |year=2016 |doi=10.2147/BTAT.S91385 |doi-access=free |url=https://www.dovepress.com/bioactive-ingredients-of-rose-hips-rosa-canina-l-with-special-referenc-peer-reviewed-fulltext-article-BTAT |access-date=2025-10-06}}</ref>

The hypanthium (fruit body) contains carotenoids (β-carotene, lycopene, lutein) and phenolics (quercetin, catechin, gallic acid), which together explain much of the fruit’s antioxidant activity.<ref>{{cite journal |last=Mármol |first=Inés |title=Therapeutic applications of rose hips from different Rosa species |journal=International Journal of Molecular Sciences |volume=18 |issue=6 |year=2017 |page=1137 |doi=10.3390/ijms18061137 |doi-access=free |pmid=28587101 |pmc=5485961 }}</ref> Variability in subspecies, environment, harvest time, and processing means that commercial rose-hip products can differ substantially in nutrient and bioactive composition unless standardized.<ref>{{cite journal |last=Patel |first=Seema |title=Rose hip as an underutilized functional food: Evidence-based review |journal=Trends in Food Science & Technology |volume=63 |pages=29–38 |year=2017 |doi=10.1016/j.tifs.2017.03.001 |url=https://doi.org/10.1016/j.tifs.2017.03.001 |access-date=2025-10-06|url-access=subscription }}</ref>

==In culture==
[[File:Hildesheim_Rosenstock.jpg|thumb|upright|The [[Thousand-year Rose]] in [[Hildesheim]]]]

The dog rose was the stylised rose of medieval European [[heraldry]].<ref>Carol Klein {{google books|yA80RgYmi-AC|Wild Flowers: Nature's own to garden grown|page=104}}</ref> It is the [[County flowers of the United Kingdom|county flower]] of [[Hampshire]],<ref name="plantlife">{{Cite web |title=Dog-rose |url=http://www.plantlife.org.uk/uk/discover-wild-plants-nature/plant-fungi-species/dog-rose |access-date=2023-03-09 |publisher=Plantlife |archive-url= https://web.archive.org/web/20230309130145/https://www.plantlife.org.uk/uk/discover-wild-plants-nature/plant-fungi-species/dog-rose |archive-date=2023-03-09 }}</ref> and Ireland's [[County Leitrim]] is nicknamed ''"The Wild Rose County"'' due to the prevalence of the dog rose in the area. Legend states the [[Thousand-year Rose]] or Hildesheim Rose, which climbs against a wall of [[Hildesheim Cathedral]], dates back to the establishment of the diocese in 815.<ref name="Vatican">{{cite web | url=http://insidethevatican.com/uncategorized/hildesheims-medieval-church-treasures-met | title=Hildesheim's Medieval Church Treasures at the Met | publisher=Inside the Vatican | access-date=30 April 2014 | author=Lucy Gordan | date=November 2013 | archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20140503122831/http://insidethevatican.com/uncategorized/hildesheims-medieval-church-treasures-met | archive-date=3 May 2014 | url-status=live}}</ref>

The first recorded significance of the flower dates back hundreds of years ago to [[Consistori del Gay Saber|The Academy of Floral Games]] (founded in 1323), which gifted poets a sprig of dog rose to reward them for their literary excellence. Due to this ritual, the branches became increasingly popular and can be found frequently mentioned in several famous poems. Most prevalent in the United Kingdom, William Shakespeare wrote about the flower in ''[[A Midsummer Night's Dream]]'',<ref name="canale">{{Cite web |last=Canale |first=Suzie |title=The Meaning of the Dog-rose |url=http://blog.exoticflowers.com/blog-0/the-meaning-of-the-dog-rose |access-date=20 November 2019 |website=blog.exoticflowers.com |language=en-us}}</ref> which in his time was called eglantine, though it can now also refer to ''Rosa rubiginosa'' (Sweet brier).<ref name="plantlife"/>

Oberon, ''A Midsummer Night's Dream'', Act II, Scene I quoting his words: "With sweet musk-roses and with eglantine."

Symbolically, the meaning of this shrub is quite extensive since the two dominating themes surrounding the flower are pain and pleasure.<ref name="canale"/>

An old riddle is called "The Five Brethren of the Rose":

''On a summer's day, in sultry weather''<br/>
''Five Brethren were born together''<br/>
''Two had beards and two had none''<br/>
''And the other had but half a one.''<ref name="stearn" />

The riddle contains an effective way of identifying the differing roses of the canina group, where the ''brethren'' refers to the five [[sepal]]s of the dog-rose, two of which are whiskered on both sides, two quite smooth and the last one whiskered on one side only.<ref name="plantlife"/>

The flower has also been used as an image on many [[postage stamps]] across Europe.{{cn|date=November 2023}}
